items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to charter schools
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S6468

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the education law, in relation to charter schools


 PURPOSE :
To improve New York's competitive position in the federal Race to the
Top grant competition by ensuring that students throughout New York
have access to quality education and school choice, further improving
the quality of charter schools, and providing school districts with
persistently under performing schools the authority to contract with
an educational management organization to help improve student
outcomes.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
Section 1:
Prohibits for-profit corporations and management companies from
applying to operate a charter school.

Section 2:
Requires charter school applicants to specify a procedure for
publicizing and conducting board meetings at the charter school.

Section 3:
Requires the code of ethics articulated in the charter school
application to include standards regarding conflicts of interest.

Section 4:
Requires that applicants seeking to open a charter school under the
RFP processes established by this legislation specifically designate
the facilities intended to be used by the charter school.  If the
intended facility changes after the submission of the application, any
necessary public hearings related to the new location must be
conducted and an amended application must submitted.

Section 5:
Designates that the terms of charters issued under the RFP process
will be five instructional years.

Section 5-a:
Makes the board of regents the sole charter entity for charter schools
issues under the RFP process; clarifies that schools may convert to
charter schools without being subject to the RFP process and that
there is no limit on the number of conversion charter schools that can
be created.

Section 6:
Clarifies that charters originally issued by a board of education, the
New York City Chancellor, and SUNY Trustees will apply to the Board of
Regents for renewal applications.

Section 6-a:
Requires charter schools applying for renewal to demonstrate the steps
they have taken to recruit and retain students at risk of educational
failure and requires that the information be included in renewal
deliberations.

Section 7:
Clarifies that the statutory deadlines for charters issued under
current law do not apply to charters issued under the RFP process.

Section 8:
Conforming language to remove reference to multiple charter entities.

Section 9:
Conforming language to make the Board of Regents responsible for
receipt of all fingerprints from prospective charter school employees.

Section 10:
Establishes that charters issued under the RFP process will be
required to include the information required by the RFP in their
proposed charter.

Section 11:
Conforming language removing references to multiple charter entities.

Section 12:
Clarifying language requiring the Board of Regents to approve charters
issued under the RFP process.

Section 13:
Establishes that charters issued under the RFP process will be
required to include the information required by the RFP in their
proposed charter.

Section 14:
Conforming language removing references to SUNY's responsibilities as
a charter entity.

Section 15:
Requires a charter revision prior to the relocation of a charter
school and requires the same level of public input as required in the
initial charter approval process.

Section 16:
Increases the number of allowable non-conversion charter schools from
200 to 400 and establishes that 200 new charters will be authorized by
under the RFP process.

Section 17:
Conforming language removing references to prior entities.

Section 18:
Establishes a RFP process by which the Board of Regents and SUNY Board
of Trustees will seek to establish a statewide plan for charter growth
to ensure that students throughout New York have access to quality
education and school choice. Requires the SUNY Board of Trustees and
Board of Regents to solicit public input prior to jointly issuing the
RFP. Requires the Boards to consider the support of the local district
as a factor in the application scoring process.

Establishes that successful applicants must demonstrate that they can
intend to recruit and will make efforts to retain high-need students.
Also requires that applicants demonstrate the acceptability of any
co-location of a charter school in another public school building to
the parents of students in the existing school building. Establishes
that applicants may apply to either the SUNY Board of Trustees or the
Board of Regents. Requires that applicants approved by the SUNY Board
of Trustees be sent to the Board of Regents for consideration.
Specifies that the SUNY Board can designate up to sixty-five charter
school applications as being highly recommended, which would result in
automatic approval by the Board of Regents. Establishes that the SUNY
Board of Trustees can approve up to half of the charters under any
individual RFP each calendar year until they reach their total of
sixty-five.

Section 19:
Conforming language removing references to multiple charter entities.

Section 20.

Establishes that charters issued under the RFP process will be issued
for five instructional years.

Section 21:
Conforming language removing references to multiple charter entities.

Section 22:
Conforming language removing references to multiple charter entities.

Section 23:  Conforming language removing references to multiple
charter entities.

Section 24:
Conforming language removing references to multiple charter entities.

Section 25:
Requires that charters issued under the RFP process be required to
comply with the same health, safety and sanitary requirements as all
other public schools. Requires localities to treat charter schools the
same as all other public schools regarding issues of zoning, land use,
and building code requirements. Allows charter schools to seek a
waiver if compliance with this section would create an undue financial
hardship or other good cause. Charter schools issued a waiver under
this section will be treated as non-public schools.

Section 26:
Allows the state to Comptroller to audit charter schools at her or his
discretion.

Section 26a:
Applies the same conflict of interest provisions and code of ethics to
charter board members, officers, and charter school employees as apply
to officers, board members and employees of public school districts.

Section 27:
Directs the Commissioner of education to create a common student
application for all charter schools and that such applications be made
available in languages predominant in the local community.  Directs to
the Commissioner to promulgate regulations to ensure that all
admission lotteries are conducted in a transparent and equitable
manner. Requires that such lotteries be held in a manner consistent
with public officers law.

Section 27a:
Clarifies that a charter school may focus its services on students in
need of special assistance, including English language learners and
students with disabilities.

Section 28:
Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 29:
Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 30:
Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 31:
Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 32:

Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 33:
Conforming legislation to eliminate references to multiple charter
entities.

Section 34:
Requires charter schools to make their annual reports more widely
available to the public through posting on the school's website,
distribution to the local newspapers and availability at charter
school board meetings. Also requires inclusion of any audits by the
State Comptroller in their annual report.

Section 35:
Requires charter school annual reports to include information
regarding the charter school's efforts to recruit and retain high-need
students during the previous school year and their plans to attract,
recruit and retain such students in the coming year.

Section 36:
Requires the annual Education Department charter school report to
include the number of charter schools that were closed in the prior
year and the reason for their closing.

Section 37:
Requires the Board of Regents to conduct an annual review of charter
school best practices and make such information available to public
school districts.

Section 38:
Technical clean-up language to strike an outdated section of law.

Section 39:
Authorizes Boards of Education to contract with educational management
organizations to assist in the turn-around of persistently low
achieving schools. Requires the Department to establish a list of
qualified not-for-profit management organizations for districts to
choose from.

 EXISTING LAW :
Under current law there are multiple charter entities; the board of
regents, the SUNY board of trustees and local school boards. Existing
law limits the number of non-conversion charter schools in New York to
200. The SUNY Board of Trustees is allowed to approve 100 charters
while the Regents and local districts are allowed to authorize an
additional 100 in total. Current law includes a geographic restriction
requiring that at least 50 of the non-SUNY charters be reserved for
the City of New York to authorize. Conversion charter schools can be
created without limit. Current law allows the Regents to approve
charter schools operated by for profit management organizations and
corporations. Current law does not require charter board members,
staff, or employees to adhere to any statutory conflict of interest
and ethical requirements such as the requirement to disclose a
financial interest in an issue before the board, recusal from action
on such issues and limitations on gifts that could be perceived to be
intended to influence an board member officer or employee. Current law
does not require that public board meetings be held at the site of the
charter school. Current law includes no specific requirements making
annual reports public.  Current law requires that charter schools make
a "good faith" effort to recruit high need students, but, there is no
process in place to monitor those efforts, or to consider the those
efforts as a part of the criteria for reauthorization. Current law
gives SED the authority to perform audits of charter schools. Current
law does not authorize of boards of education to contract with
educational management organizations.
 JUSTIFICATION :  The federal Race to the Top grant competition will
award funding to a select number of states with educational policies
that encourage the growth of high quality charter schools and provide
options for school district officials seeking to turn around low
performing schools.  This legislation seeks to enhance New York's
competitiveness by increasing the charter school cap while promoting a
thoughtful statewide approach to charter school growth. This approach
will provide equitable access to a greater variety of students, and
greater educational benefit to all students.

To date, charter schools in New York have largely succeeded in
providing access to high-quality, public educational alternatives to
traditional school systems. Unfortunately, the current system of
authorizing charters has resulted in an uneven distribution of charter
school opportunities across grade levels and throughout the state.
This legislation reforms the chartering process to allow the SUNY
Board of Trustees and Board of Regents to jointly issue competitive
request for proposals which will allow them to award charters to most
innovative and highest quality applicants. The SUNY Board and Regents
could also use the RFP process to grant charters to applicants seeking
to enhance options for students left unserved by the current system.

This legislation will also require charter schools to be more
accountable with regard to their responsibility to recruit and retain
high needs students. The successful programs in charter schools should
be made available to the students who most need the assistance and
opportunities that these innovative programs provide.

This legislation will also enhance the public's confidence in charter
schools by allowing for audits by the state comptroller and by
requiring charter board members to meet the same conflict of interest
and ethical obligations as elected school board members. The bill
would also help ensure that tax dollars be used for educating students
to the greatest extent possible by granting future charters solely to
not-for-profit charter school operators.

Requiring a common application for all charter schools will simplify
the process for parents seeking to enroll their child in a charter
school while requiring that charter school applications be printed in
the community's most common languages helps English language learners
with the enrollment process. Creating an open process for charter
school lotteries will also enhance public confidence in the charter
school lottery process where applicable.

This bill also requires greater distribution of information about
charter schools, including posting of audits and publicizing the
efforts to recruit and retain students who need academic support.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
This is a new bill.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
This legislation will enhance New York's Race to the Top federal grant
application which could provide the State Education Department and
public schools with between $350 and $700 million if New York should
win an award. The State Education Department could incur some
additional costs related to the administration and oversight to new
and renewing charters.

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
Local school districts will incur a tuition expense for each student
that chooses a charter school.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This legislation takes effect immediately except for sections six,
six-a, eight, nine, eleven, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, seventeen,
nineteen, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four,
twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one,
thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-five and thirty-eight which take
effect January 1, 2011.
